analysis.one_liner: Bans race-based preferences in federal hiring, contracting, and federally funded programs.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 10 Republican sponsors in January 2025, has sat in four House committees with no action since referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The FAIR Act would bar the federal government — and any state, school, or company that receives federal money — from either discriminating against or giving any preference based on race, color, or national origin in contracts, hiring, or college admissions. It treats a preference as any advantage of a kind, including quotas, set-asides, and numerical goals, and would let any person harmed sue in court and collect attorney's fees. Federal agencies would have six months to rewrite their rules to comply.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who believes they lost out on a federal job, contract, license, or college admission because of a race-conscious program — regardless of their own race — could sue and recover attorney's fees. Institutions that already operate race-blind would face no change.

how_it_helps.text: It creates a private right of action: any person aggrieved by a violation can sue the violator, including a government entity, and a winning plaintiff gets reasonable attorney's fees.
It defines 'preference' to include quotas, set-asides, numerical goals, timetables, or other numerical objectives, so programs that reserve spots or set numeric targets by race would be off-limits.
Federal agencies would have to review all their policies and regulations within six months of enactment and modify them to conform, reporting results to the Judiciary Committees.

analysis.who_pays: Federal agencies, contractors, and schools would have to dismantle race-conscious programs — including set-asides and numeric goals designed to counteract past or present discrimination — and could face lawsuits. Beneficiaries of those programs would lose the opportunities they provided.
analysis.who_pays_short: Agencies, contractors, and schools with such programs

drawbacks.text: The bill would bar not just discrimination but remedial programs: it outlaws preferences including set-asides and numerical goals, so tools designed to counteract discrimination — such as minority business contracting programs — would lose their legal basis, not just illegal discrimination.

It reaches private and state entities that receive any federal financial assistance, covering employment, contracts, and college admissions, a far broader scope than federal anti-discrimination law now requires of them.
The new private right of action with mandatory attorney's fees would invite litigation against agencies, contractors, and schools over any race-related decision or program.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's appeal is a colorblind rule: government never treats anyone differently by race, and anyone hurt can sue. The cost is that it removes race-conscious remedies along with race-conscious discrimination, ending programs that some people rely on and creating a new wave of lawsuits against schools and agencies. Whether that is a fair trade depends on how one weighs individual colorblind treatment against the value of programs aimed at counteracting discrimination.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees the day it was introduced, and none has taken it up since.

narrative.text: The FAIR Act was introduced in the House on January 23, 2025, by Rep. Thomas Tiffany with eight cosponsors, all Republicans.
It was referred the same day to four committees — Judiciary, Oversight and Government Reform, Education and Workforce, and House Administration.
No committee has reported the bill, and no further action appears in the record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo holds: race-conscious federal programs continue to operate, and no one has had to change practices or face the bill's new lawsuits. Members who introduced it gain a statement on the record without needing to move it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbent programs and the status quo

for.name: 9 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction: Owens, Tenney, Hageman, Ogles, Miller of Illinois, Grothman, Weber of Texas, and Moore of Alabama.

against.name: House committee chairs
against.role: Chairs of the Judiciary, Oversight, Education and Workforce, and House Administration committees
against.what_they_did: Have not scheduled any markup or action on the bill since it was referred on January 23, 2025.

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors and cosponsors are House Republicans; no Democrat has joined.

industries.industry: Federal contractors and grantees with race-conscious programs
industries.note: Contractors that operate diversity set-asides or numeric goals on federal work would have to end them, while those preferring no race-related requirements would gain certainty. The bill would apply to any company or state entity taking federal money, not just direct contractors.

Institutions receiving federal aid could not grant any race-based preference in admissions, employment, or contracts. Some schools had already ended race-conscious admissions after court rulings; the bill would extend the ban to employment and contracting and open them to suits.

industries.industry: Government contractors with small or disadvantaged business set-asides
industries.note: Race-conscious contracting set-asides, which channel federal work to firms owned by minority group members, fall squarely under the bill's definition of a preference and would lose their legal footing, removing a source of federal revenue for those firms.

analysis.trajectory: With no committee action in months, all-Republican sponsorship, and four committees sharing jurisdiction, the bill is very unlikely to advance this Congress; bills at this stage typically die quietly when session ends.
